newsitem.title: GERMANY: German 1997 tax shortfall estimate 18 bln marks.
newsitem.headline: German 1997 tax shortfall estimate 18 bln marks.

text.p: Government and private tax experts on Thursday estimated that 1997 tax revenues would be 18 billion marks less than previously believed, dealing a blow to German efforts to qualify for the single European currency.

The new estimate sees 1997 German tax revenues on the federal, state and local levels, including funds collected for transfer to the European Union, at 813.1 billion marks. After correcting for changes in tax laws, that is 18 billion marks less than the previous estimate last November.
Federal tax revenues alone are seen at 336.7 billion marks in 1997, 9.1 billion marks less than last time.
For 1998, overall tax revenues are now seen at 843.5 billion marks, 31.6 billion marks short of the previous estimate. Federal revenues are seen at 348.4 billion marks, down 14.6 billion.

The estimates, drawn up in a three-day, closed-door semiannual session in Schwerin by finance officials from federal, state and local governments as well as private-sector advisors, form the basis of future fiscal planning.
Finance Minister Theo Waigel said the new estimate would not affect Germany's chances of qualifying for European monetary union.
The decision of which countries are to participate in EMU at the January 1999 start is to be made in one year, based on 1997 data.
But opposition Social Democrat leader Oskar Lafontaine said the budget gap shows Chancellor Helmut Kohl's tax plans are out of step with reality.
